To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a LiNO3/N,N-dimethyle acetamide (DMA) electrolyte is compatible with the Li anode and the O2 electrode and can sustain > 80 cycles of Li-O2 battery operation.

a Li-O(3) cell containing a LiNO(3)-DMA electrolyte is shown to cycle successfully for more than 80 cycles at a current density 0.1mA/cm2 with a consistent charging voltage profile, good capacity and Coulombic efficiency retention, and O2 as the primary gassed product formed during charge.

the addition of lithium nitrate to an N,N-dimethlyacetamide-based electrolyte enables stable cycling of the Li metal anode, and that the resulting Li-O(2)-based battery can be charged and discharged repeatedly with high coulombic efficiency.

the development of rechargeble Li-O(2), batteries that are based on an electrolyte composed of LiNO(3) and DMA.
the development of rechargea Li-O2 batteries are promising candidates for high-energy storage devices.
the development of new Li-O(2)-based rechargeable batteries with high energy density.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this electrolyte composition, consisting of DMA and LiNO(3) in a 1:1 ratio, provides a new and promising approach for developing rechargeable Li-O-2 batteries.
the Li-O(2)/LiNO(3)-DMA cell is a rechargeable battery with a high capacity, long cycling life, and good coulombic and energy efficiency.
the use of lithium nitrate in a Li-O2 cell with an N,N-dimethlyacetamide solvent has been demonstrated for the first time to provide stable cycling with a Li anode and O(2)-evolving electrode.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have discovered a new class of electrolytes that is suitable for both the cathode and anode in a Li-air cell.
the use of lithium nitrate as a salt in the electrolyte allows the Li anode to be cycled in a polar solvent, such as DMA.

the electrolyte system of LiNO(3)/DMA is the first electrolyte system to cycle a Li metal anode and an O(2) cathode for more than 1000 cycles with a stable charging voltage and a stable discharge voltage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of LiNO(3) with DMA is a viable alternative to using LiPF(6) with dimethyl sulfoxide for the development of a Li-O( 2) battery.
the presence of a stable SEI on the Li anodes in Li-O(2)-type cells is a critical requirement for achieving long-term cycling stability.
LiNO(3) can stabilize Li metal in the presence of DMA, a solvent that is otherwise unstable in the presence of a Li anolyte.
